items.stem: Define a vector quantity.
items.answer: A quantity that has both magnitude and direction, such as displacement or velocity
items.markingKey: 1 mark: A vector quantity – a quantity that has both magnitude and direction, such as displacement or velocity.

items.stem: Displacement can be zero when the distance travelled is:
items.answer: not zero, if the object returns to its starting point
items.markingKey: (b) not zero, if the object returns to its starting point.
options: not zero, if the object returns to its starting point

items.stem:
Assertion (A): An object can have zero displacement but non-zero distance.
Reason (R): Displacement depends only on the initial and final positions.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: Riya walks 3 m due east and then 4 m due north. Find the distance travelled and the magnitude of the displacement.
items.markingKey: Distance = 3 + 4 = 7 m. Displacement = √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5 m (north-east of start).

items.stem: An athlete runs one and a half rounds of a circular track of radius 7 m. Find the distance covered and the magnitude of displacement. (Take π = 22/7.)
items.markingKey: Circumference = 2πr = 2 × 22/7 × 7 = 44 m; distance = 1.5 × that = 66 m. Displacement is the straight line from start to finish = 14 m.

items.stem: An athlete runs a quarter of a round of a circular track of radius 7 m. Find the distance covered and the magnitude of displacement. (Take π = 22/7.)
items.markingKey: Circumference = 2πr = 2 × 22/7 × 7 = 44 m; distance = 0.25 × that = 11 m. Displacement is the straight line from start to finish = 9.9 m.

items.stem: Why is it necessary to mention a reference point when describing motion?
items.answer: Motion is relative: an object may be moving with respect to one object and at rest with respect to another.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: relative. 1 mark: example or reasoning.

items.stem: A passenger sitting in a moving bus is at rest with respect to:
options: a person standing at the bus stop

items.stem: Mehak walks 8 km due east and then 15 km due north. Find the distance travelled and the magnitude of the displacement.
items.markingKey: Distance = 8 + 15 = 23 km. Displacement = √(8² + 15²) = √289 = 17 km (north-east of start).

items.stem: Define speed.
items.answer: The distance travelled by an object in unit time
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Speed – the distance travelled by an object in unit time.

items.stem: Convert a speed of 90 km/h into m/s.
A swimmer swims one length of a 100 m pool in 25 s and returns to the start in 25 s. Find her average speed and average velocity for the whole swim.
items.answer: Average speed 4 m/s; average velocity 0 m/s
items.markingKey: (b) Average speed = 200 ÷ 50 = 4 m/s. Displacement is zero (back at start), so average velocity = 0.
options: Average speed 2 m/s; average velocity 0 m/s
Average speed 4 m/s; average velocity 0 m/s
Average speed 4 m/s; average velocity 4 m/s
Average speed 0 m/s; average velocity 4 m/s

items.stem: A cyclist covers 100 m in 200 s. What is the average speed in m/s and in km/h?
A swimmer swims one length of a 200 m pool in 30 s and returns to the start in 40 s. Find her average speed and average velocity for the whole swim.
items.answer: Average speed 5.71 m/s; average velocity 0 m/s
items.markingKey: Average speed = 400 ÷ 70 = 5.71 m/s. Displacement is zero (back at start), so average velocity = 0.

items.stem: Dev's family drives 30 km (Delhi to Meerut) at 60 km/h and returns the same distance at 40 km/h. Find the average speed for the whole trip.
items.markingKey: Time = 30/60 + 30/40 = 1.25 h; average speed = total distance ÷ total time = 60 ÷ 1.25 = 48 km/h (not the mean of the speeds).

items.stem: Ananya's family drives 60 km (Lucknow to Kanpur) at 40 km/h and returns the same distance at 60 km/h. Find the average speed for the whole trip.
items.markingKey: Time = 60/40 + 60/60 = 2.5 h; average speed = total distance ÷ total time = 120 ÷ 2.5 = 48 km/h (not the mean of the speeds).

items.stem:
Read: Farhan cycles around a circular park of radius 35 m at a steady speed, taking 44 s for each round.
(i) Find the distance covered in one round (π = 22/7). (ii) Find the speed. (iii) What is the displacement after one complete round? (iv) Is Farhan accelerating? Explain.
items.answer: (i) 220 m. (ii) 5 m/s. (iii) Zero. (iv) Yes, the direction of motion keeps changing, so velocity changes.

items.stem: Convert a speed of 108 km/h into m/s.
Convert a speed of 18 km/h into m/s.
Convert a speed of 126 km/h into m/s.
The SI unit of acceleration is:
A car speeds up from 20 m/s to 35 m/s in 4 s. Find its acceleration.

Assertion (A): A body moving in a circle with constant speed is accelerated.
Reason (R): The direction of its velocity keeps changing.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: A train starting with velocity 4 m/s moves with uniform acceleration 2.5 m/s². How far does it travel in 2 s?
A bus moving at 15 m/s applies brakes and stops in 5 s with uniform retardation. Find the retardation and the distance travelled while braking.
items.markingKey: a = (0 − 15)/5 = −3 m/s² (retardation 3 m/s²); s = ut + ½at² = 15 × 5 − ½ × 3 × 5² = 37.5 m.

items.stem: A car moving at 72 km/h on an expressway brakes with a uniform retardation of 3 m/s². Find (i) the time taken to stop and (ii) the stopping distance.

Read: Meera recorded the speedometer reading of a car on a straight road every second after it left a toll plaza. It started at 0 m/s and its speed rose by 2 m/s every second for 6 s.
(i) Is the motion uniform or non-uniform? (ii) What is the acceleration? (iii) Find the speed at t = 6 s. (iv) Find the distance covered in these 6 s.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each: (iii) v = u + at; (iv) s = ut + ½at² = 0 × 6 + ½ × 2 × 6² = 36 m.

items.stem: A car moving at 72 km/h on an expressway brakes with a uniform retardation of 5 m/s². Find (i) the time taken to stop and (ii) the stopping distance.
Two cars start together from a signal. Car A accelerates at 2 m/s² from rest; car B moves at a constant 10 m/s. When and where will A catch up with B?
items.answer: A: s = ½ × 2 × t² = t²; B: s = 10t; equal when t² = 10t, t = 10 s; distance = 100 m.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each equation. 1 mark: t = 10 s and 100 m.

items.stem: A car speeds up from 10 m/s to 25 m/s in 8 s. Find its acceleration.
A car speeds up from 5 m/s to 15 m/s in 2 s. Find its acceleration.
Can an object have zero velocity and non-zero acceleration at the same moment? Give an example.
items.answer: Yes: a ball thrown upwards at its highest point has zero velocity but acceleration due to gravity downwards.

items.stem: The slope of a velocity–time graph gives:
A velocity–time graph is a straight line from 10 m/s at t = 0 to 20 m/s at t = 10 s. Find the acceleration and the distance travelled in this time.
items.markingKey: (a) Slope = (20 − 10)/10 = 1 m/s². Area under graph = ½ × (10 + 20) × 10 = 150 m.

items.stem: Two distance–time graphs A and B are straight lines through the origin; A is steeper. Which object is faster? Explain.
items.answer: A, because the slope of a distance–time graph is the speed, and A has the greater slope.

items.stem: A velocity–time graph is a straight line from 5 m/s at t = 0 to 25 m/s at t = 8 s. Find the acceleration and the distance travelled in this time.
items.markingKey: Slope = (25 − 5)/8 = 2.5 m/s². Area under graph = ½ × (5 + 25) × 8 = 120 m.

items.stem: Arjun records the position of a toy car every second: 0 m, 5 m, 10 m, 15 m, 20 m. Is the motion uniform? What will the distance–time graph look like, and what is the speed?
items.answer: Uniform motion; a straight line through the origin; speed 5 m/s.
items.markingKey: Equal distances (5 m) in equal times, so uniform; slope = 5 m/s (2 marks).

items.stem: A metro train starts from rest, accelerates uniformly to 20 m/s in 10 s, runs at this speed for 20 s, and then stops uniformly in 5 s. Using a velocity–time graph, find the total distance and the average speed.
The distance–time graph of a delivery rider is a straight line from 0 to 10 min, flat from 10 to 15 min, and then a steeper straight line to 25 min. Describe the motion in each part.
items.answer: 0–10 min: uniform speed; 10–15 min: at rest (stopped); 15–25 min: uniform motion at a higher speed than before.

items.stem: A metro train starts from rest, accelerates uniformly to 10 m/s in 2 s, runs at this speed for 8 s, and then stops uniformly in 4 s. Using a velocity–time graph, find the total distance and the average speed.

Assertion (A): The distance–time graph of an object at rest is parallel to the time axis.
Reason (R): The position of an object at rest does not change with time.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: A velocity–time graph is a straight line from 10 m/s at t = 0 to 30 m/s at t = 5 s. Find the acceleration and the distance travelled in this time.
items.markingKey: (b) Slope = (30 − 10)/5 = 4 m/s². Area under graph = ½ × (10 + 30) × 5 = 100 m.

items.stem: A ball is dropped from a height. Sketch (describe) its velocity–time graph and say what the slope and area represent.
items.answer: A straight line through the origin rising with time (uniform acceleration ≈ 9.8 m/s²); slope = acceleration due to gravity; area = distance fallen.
items.markingKey: 1 mark shape. 1 mark slope. 1 mark area.

items.stem: Define centripetal direction.
items.answer: The direction towards the centre of the circle in circular motion
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Centripetal direction – the direction towards the centre of the circle in circular motion.

A cyclist goes once around a circular track of radius 105 m in 11 s. Find its speed. (π = 22/7)
A satellite moves in a circular orbit of radius 42250 km and completes one orbit in 24 h. Calculate its speed in km/s.
An object is moving at a constant 20 m/s. Is it necessarily in uniform motion? Explain with two cases.
items.answer: Not necessarily. On a straight road at constant speed it has uniform velocity; on a circular track at the same speed its direction changes, so its velocity changes and it is accelerating.
